facts.text: On this date in 1993, the Oslo Accords were signed — a handshake on the White House lawn between Rabin and Arafat watched by 3,000 guests and a billion people on television.

On this date in 1759, the Battle of the Plains of Abraham lasted just 15 minutes but permanently shifted North America's political language — French Canada survives today as a direct consequence of the peace terms, not the battle.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth, with over 111,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any Manhattan block, averaged across the entire city.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, holding roughly 60% of the world's total lake water by surface area.

The United Arab Emirates imports nearly all of its food — over 90% — despite being one of the wealthiest nations per capita, making its supermarkets among the most geopolitically fragile on the planet.

On this date in 1992, George Soros broke the Bank of England, shorting the pound so aggressively that Britain was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. He pocketed roughly $1 billion in a single day.

On September 13, 2008, Lehman Brothers executives met at the New York Fed in a last-ditch attempt to find a buyer. No deal materialized, and the firm filed for the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history two days later.

The Dutch East India Company, often cited as the world's first publicly traded corporation, was at its peak worth an estimated $8 trillion in today's dollars — more than the current combined market cap of Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia.
The S&P 500 has historically risen more on Fridays than any other weekday, a pattern so persistent that quantitative traders have a name for it: the weekend effect. No one has fully explained it.

Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway once traded a single Class A share for over $700,000 — making it the most expensive publicly listed stock in history, deliberately never split so that short-term speculators would stay away.

On this date in 1922, Al Azizia, Libya recorded 58°C — a temperature hot enough to cook an egg on the ground. That record stood for 90 years before scientists discovered the measurement was taken over asphalt, not natural ground.
On September 13, 1959, Luna 2 became the first human-made object to reach another world, crashing into the Moon at 3.3 km/s. It carried no camera — its only job was to arrive.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A single teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces the lining of your small intestine every two to four days. The organ doing the most work in keeping you alive is also among the fastest to rebuild itself.
Light leaving the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth, but it spent up to 100,000 years fighting its way from the Sun's core to its surface before that journey even began.
On this day in 1916, Roald Dahl was born. He didn't publish his first children's book until he was 45 — older than the entire history of commercial television.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramids were already 2,500 years old when she was born.
On this day in 1948, Margaret Chase Smith became the first woman to win a U.S. presidential primary. The transistor had just been invented six months earlier.
Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire by roughly 200 years. When Montezuma was crowned, Oxford had already been teaching for three centuries.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — 33 years before Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone. We invented a way to send documents before we could send voices.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Now used as if it were ancient.
Hiraeth (Welsh, n.): a longing for a home you cannot return to, or that never existed. Untranslatable into English, it folds homesickness, grief, and nostalgia into a single ache.
On this day in 1321, Dante Alighieri died in Ravenna. The word 'treacle' descends from his era's theriaca — an antidote to poison — which is precisely how sweetness entered the language of medicine.

Mamihlapinatapai: a Yaghan word from Tierra del Fuego meaning the look shared between two people who both want something but neither will initiate. The Yaghan language now has one fluent native speaker.
Sillage (French, n.): the scent trail left in the air by a passing person. From the nautical word for a ship's wake. Perfumers rate fragrances by it. English simply has no equivalent.

On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal and ordered all completed ones refunded — wiping out roughly $400M in token sales within 48 hours and triggering Bitcoin's sharpest single-week drop of that year.

On this date in 2018, Ethereum's Ropsten testnet was successfully used to rehearse the then-upcoming Constantinople hard fork, a dry run that later caught a critical reentrancy bug before it hit mainnet.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named by Satoshi Nakamoto — it was proposed by a forum user in 2010 and adopted by the community while Nakamoto was still actively posting.

The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit a bug in Ethereum itself — it exploited a reentrancy vulnerability in a third-party contract, yet Ethereum forked anyway, establishing that social consensus can override immutability.

Bitcoin's 21 million supply cap is enforced by integer arithmetic, not a hard-coded constant — miners' block rewards are halved by right-shifting a 64-bit integer, and after 64 halvings the shift produces zero, making new issuance mathematically impossible.
On this date in 2012, AlexNet's ImageNet submission was being finalized — it would cut the top-5 error rate from 26% to 15.3%, a gap so large the field assumed the results were wrong.
On this date in 1956, the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was winding down — the term 'artificial intelligence' itself was coined just to secure the grant funding.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US homes, spent on a single model.

Transformers now underpin nearly every frontier AI system, yet the original 2017 paper was rejected from ICLR before being accepted at NeurIPS — three of its eight authors left Google within two years.
AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — more than humanity had experimentally determined in the entire prior history of structural biology — in under a year of deployment.
